# Stablecoins are the tokenization that already won

Tokenization gets pitched as something coming for Treasuries, gold, and real estate. By the only metric that counts — value actually moved on-chain — it already happened, years ago, and the asset that won was the dollar.

ST [Swop Team](https://www.swopme.co/blog/authors/swop-team) Nov 10, 2026 Updated Nov 10, 2026 7 min read Copy link [X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Stablecoins%20are%20the%20tokenization%20that%20already%20won&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fstablecoins-already-won-tokenization) [Farcaster](https://warpcast.com/~/compose?text=Stablecoins%20are%20the%20tokenization%20that%20already%20won&embeds[]=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fstablecoins-already-won-tokenization)

Contents What counts as tokenization The numbers nobody states side by side Why stablecoins won first What "winning" doesn’t mean Where this goes next FAQ

A stablecoin is tokenization: a token issued against a reserve of dollars or dollar-equivalent assets held off-chain, redeemable against that reserve, and transferable on a public blockchain. Judged by that definition, stablecoins are not a preview of real-world-asset tokenization — they are its largest result to date. About $290 billion in stablecoins circulate on-chain today, against roughly $32–48 billion for every other tokenized real-world asset combined — Treasuries, gold, private credit, real estate. The asset everyone keeps describing as "about to be tokenized" already was, and it was cash.

That gap matters for anyone trying to read where tokenization is actually headed, because the industry's own numbers keep answering a different question than the one usually asked.

## What counts as tokenization

Strip away the branding and a tokenized asset is always the same shape: a claim and a redemption right on something that lives off-chain, represented by a token that moves on a public ledger instead of in a bank's or registrar's private database. Tokenized gold, like [PAX Gold](https://www.paxos.com/pax-gold), is a claim on physical gold held in a vault. A tokenized Treasury fund is a claim on a basket of government debt. A dollar-backed stablecoin is a claim on a reserve of dollars and short-term dollar instruments, redeemable 1:1.

None of that is a metaphor. It is the literal structure every tracker uses when it adds up "tokenized real-world assets," and under that structure, stablecoins are not kept in a separate bucket from Treasuries or gold — they are the biggest line item inside the same bucket.

## The numbers nobody states side by side

Figures differ by tracker and by week, because different trackers include different token sets and measure distributed value differently from represented value. But every major source — including [DefiLlama's live stablecoin tracker](https://defillama.com/stablecoins) — lands in the same place: stablecoins are not comparable in size to the rest of tokenized real-world assets — they dwarf them.

~$290B

Stablecoins outstanding

~$32–48B

Every other tokenized RWA, combined

~86%

Stablecoin share of on-chain tokenized value

[CoinDesk Data's July 2026 report](https://data.coindesk.com/reports/stablecoins-tokenized-assets-report-july-2026) put total stablecoin market capitalization at roughly $308 billion, against $32.1 billion for non-stablecoin tokenized real-world assets — the highest level that second figure had ever reached. A separate Token Terminal breakdown from the same quarter put total on-chain tokenized value at about $346 billion, with stablecoins making up roughly 86% of it and the remainder — led by tokenized Treasuries at around $15 billion — split across every other category.

Non-stablecoin tokenization is not standing still. [CoinGecko's research desk](https://www.coingecko.com/learn/what-are-real-world-assets-exploring-rwa-protocols) recorded tokenized RWAs excluding stablecoins growing 256.7% over fifteen months, from $5.42 billion in January 2025 to $19.32 billion by the end of Q1 2026 — a real growth rate by any standard. It is also, on CoinGecko's own framing, still only about 6.4% the size of the stablecoin market, up from 2.7% a year earlier — fast growth off a small base. For a live view of how the categories currently split, [RWA.xyz's public tracker](https://app.rwa.xyz/) breaks out tokenized Treasuries, private credit, and commodities separately from stablecoins.

## Why stablecoins won first

The gap is not an accident of timing. Stablecoins had a structural head start that tokenized Treasuries and gold do not share.

Demand for dollars is already universal. A stablecoin does not need to create a market — it only needs to move an existing one onto a rail that settles faster and moves more easily across borders than a bank account does. We wrote about that rail property on its own terms in [Settlement is the product](https://www.swopme.co/blog/settlement-is-the-product): the thing tokenization changes first is not what the asset is, it’s how long it takes to actually have it.

Tokenized Treasuries and gold carry more friction before they can even compete. Most are gated to accredited or institutional buyers, and most route through a transfer-agent or allowlist layer that decides who is permitted to hold the token at all — the exact dynamic we covered in [Tokenized isn’t the same as yours](https://www.swopme.co/blog/tokenized-isnt-the-same-as-yours). A token that reverts if it lands in the wrong wallet is solving a compliance problem before it can solve a convenience problem. A dollar stablecoin, for the large majority of its users, has no such gate.

There’s also a simpler reason: most people who want gold or Treasury exposure can already get it through an existing brokerage account with a few taps. Tokenization has to beat an incumbent that is already easy to use. Cross-border dollar access is the opposite case — for a large share of the world, the existing option is genuinely bad, which is exactly the gap stablecoins stepped into first.

## What "winning" doesn’t mean

None of this means a stablecoin and a dollar are the same thing, and it’s worth being precise about where the analogy stops.

Holding a stablecoin means holding a claim on an issuer's promise to redeem it, backed by a reserve that issuer controls and reports on. That claim is only as good as the reserve, the audits behind it, and the issuer's own solvency — the identical counterparty question that applies to a tokenized Treasury fund or a tokenized gold bar. Tokenization moved the asset onto a faster, more transferable rail. It did not remove the issuer sitting in the middle of the claim, and it did not make every stablecoin interchangeable: different issuers carry different reserve composition, different audit cadence, and different jurisdictional backstops, which is the same "custody is the real variable" point this blog has made about tokenized RWAs generally.

This is a market-structure observation about tokenization broadly, not a claim about any stablecoin Swop issues — Swop doesn’t issue one.

## Where this goes next

If stablecoins are the proof of concept, the rest of tokenization is trying to repeat the trick for assets that don’t have a built-in global market waiting for them. McKinsey’s tokenization outlook — which, like the trackers above, counts tokenized financial assets excluding stablecoins and cryptocurrencies — put that market at roughly $2 trillion by 2030 in its base case, about $4 trillion in a bullish one, and nearer $1 trillion if adoption stays slow. Treat the range as directional rather than precise: it dates from 2024, and every forecaster defines the category differently, as the trackers above already show for today's numbers.

What that next wave borrows from stablecoins is the part that actually mattered: an asset you can hold yourself, move without asking permission, and settle instantly, rather than one that is merely described on a blockchain while the real custody arrangement stays exactly as it was. [USDC, USDC.e and pUSD](https://www.swopme.co/blog/usdc-vs-usdce) already show that even within "the tokenization that won," which specific token you’re holding still matters.

Swop sits on the self-custody side of that question for whichever tokenized asset you’re holding. You control your Swop wallet: nothing moves without your approval, you can export your private key, and Swop never holds your keys. Wallets run on Privy today, and Swop runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base, and Polygon, so stablecoins on any of those chains sit in a wallet you control rather than an account someone else administers. Transactions on Swop are gas-sponsored — you don’t need to hold SOL or ETH to transact — which matters here because moving a stablecoin you already hold shouldn’t require first acquiring a second asset just to pay the fee. Swop has a built-in swap: you get a quote and sign inside the app, without sending funds to an exchange or connecting to a separate site; Swop routes Solana swaps through Jupiter and EVM swaps through LiFi. And the next wave of tokenized real-world assets isn’t hypothetical on Swop either: tokenized real-world assets that live on Swop's supported chains — such as PAX Gold (PAXG) on Ethereum — can be swapped in the Swop app through its existing routing, the same as any other token on that chain.

## FAQ

### Are stablecoins a form of real-world-asset tokenization?

Yes, by the same definition used for tokenized Treasuries or gold: a token issued against a reserve of a real-world asset held off-chain, redeemable against that reserve, and transferable on a public blockchain. A dollar-backed stablecoin is a token issued against a reserve of dollars or dollar-equivalents, redeemable 1:1. Trackers that measure tokenized real-world assets generally count stablecoins as the largest category of that market, not a separate one.

### Why have stablecoins grown so much faster than tokenized Treasuries or gold?

Demand for dollars is already universal, so a stablecoin doesn’t have to create a market, only move an existing one onto a faster rail. Tokenized Treasuries and gold have to do more work first: most are gated to accredited or institutional buyers, require a transfer-agent or allowlist layer to enforce who may hold the token, and are competing against an off-chain version of the same asset that most buyers can already access.

### Does holding a stablecoin mean you own a dollar?

No. It means you hold a claim on an issuer who promises to redeem your token for a dollar from its reserve. That claim is only as good as the issuer's reserve, its audits, and its own solvency — the same counterparty question that applies to tokenized Treasuries or gold. Tokenization moves the asset onto a faster, more transferable rail; it does not remove the issuer in the middle.

### Can I hold and swap stablecoins in a self-custody wallet?

Yes. You control your Swop wallet: nothing moves without your approval, you can export your private key, and Swop never holds your keys. Wallets run on Privy today, and Swop runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base, and Polygon. Swop has a built-in swap: you get a quote and sign inside the app, without sending funds to an exchange or connecting to a separate site; Swop routes Solana swaps through Jupiter and EVM swaps through LiFi. Transactions on Swop are gas-sponsored — you don’t need to hold SOL or ETH to transact.

# What happens if a tokenized asset’s issuer fails?

The chain keeps an honest record of your balance. It has no vote in what you actually recover if the issuer behind the token goes under — that depends on paperwork most holders never read.

ST [Swop Team](https://www.swopme.co/blog/authors/swop-team) Nov 10, 2026 Updated Nov 10, 2026 7 min read Copy link [X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=What%20happens%20if%20a%20tokenized%20asset%27s%20issuer%20fails%3F&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Ftokenized-asset-issuer-fails) [Farcaster](https://warpcast.com/~/compose?text=What%20happens%20if%20a%20tokenized%20asset%27s%20issuer%20fails%3F&embeds[]=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Ftokenized-asset-issuer-fails)

Contents The chain records it. It doesn't decide it Three structures, three different outcomes What actually decides the outcome What self-custody does and doesn't change Where Swop fits FAQ

If the issuer of your tokenized real-world asset goes bankrupt or otherwise fails, what you get back depends on the legal structure behind the token — not on the blockchain it runs on. Some issuers hold customer assets in a segregated, bankruptcy-remote structure that sits outside their own estate; others leave holders with an unsecured claim that competes with the issuer's other creditors, and whose payout can be paused, reduced, or deferred under the token's own terms. A tokenized asset is a claim on whoever issued it, and that claim is only as strong as the paperwork behind it.

## The chain records it. It doesn't decide it

It is tempting to treat "it's on-chain" as a safety feature. The blockchain does one thing reliably: it keeps an accurate, tamper-resistant record of who holds how many units of a token. That record will still be perfectly accurate the day an issuer files for bankruptcy. It will also be almost entirely beside the point, because the record answers "who holds the token," not "what is the token actually worth, and to whom."

We covered the first half of this problem in [a companion piece on custody](https://www.swopme.co/blog/tokenized-isnt-the-same-as-yours): whether you can even move a tokenized asset to a wallet you control is a choice the issuer made, not a property of being on-chain. Issuer failure is the second half, and the harder one, because it survives even when you clear the first hurdle. You can hold a tokenized asset in a wallet nobody but you controls and still be an unsecured creditor the moment its issuer goes under.

## Three structures, three different outcomes

The clearest real-world example of a deliberately strong structure is Paxos’s gold token, PAX Gold (PAXG). Paxos has argued for years that a trust charter — rather than a money-transmitter licence — is what actually protects customers. In [its own account of its bankruptcy protections](https://www.paxos.com/blog/paxos-was-built-to-protect-its-customers), written while it was a New York limited-purpose trust company, it said customer assets are held segregated and bankruptcy-remote, never commingled with corporate funds, and that an insolvency would not go through standard bankruptcy procedure at all: the NYDFS Superintendent would return custodied assets to their owners directly, based on Paxos’s books and records. The contrast it drew was with money-transmitter-licensed issuers, whose customers it said could face delays and a court ruling that their assets belong to the issuer’s bankruptcy estate.

That charter has since changed — and pinning down how far it has changed is this post in miniature. Paxos says it [completed its conversion to a national trust bank charter on December 12, 2025](https://www.paxos.com/blog/occ-charter-stablecoins), and that it now operates as Paxos Trust Company, N.A., with PAXG issued by that entity — issuance, reserves and custody all sitting inside it. The [OCC’s own action that day](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2025/nr-occ-2025-125.html) was a conditional approval, one of five granted to crypto firms, and its decision lists a Conversion Completion Acknowledgement as the step that authorises a converted bank to begin business. We could not find an OCC notice confirming that step for Paxos, and a February 2026 OCC corporate decision still refers to the conversion as a conditional approval. The segregated, bankruptcy-remote framing carries over in Paxos’s telling either way, but which supervisor’s insolvency mechanism would actually run — New York’s Superintendent or the federal regime — is not something a holder can settle from either party’s public materials. That is the whole argument of this post arriving in its own flagship example: the thing that decides your recovery is a charter, and the charter is genuinely hard to pin down. A holder who read the earlier Paxos page and stopped there is carrying a picture the issuer has since revised; a holder who reads only the new one is taking a company’s word on its own regulatory status.

BlackRock's tokenized Treasury fund, BUIDL, sits on different rails. Per [the fund's 2024 launch announcement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240320771318/en/), Bank of New York Mellon serves as custodian of the fund's assets and administrator, while Securitize acts as transfer agent and tokenization platform recording who holds the tokenized shares. That is a conventional fund structure with an independent, regulated custodian holding the underlying Treasuries and cash — a meaningfully different arrangement from an issuer custodying its own backing asset. Whether BUIDL's specific legal claim is formally bankruptcy-remote in the way Paxos describes for PAXG is a question for the fund's own offering documents, which we did not have access to verify directly.

Not every tokenized asset gets either kind of protection. Industry risk assessments of the broader RWA tokenization market describe a less reassuring pattern elsewhere: pooled custody accounts without clear segregation, commingled cash management, and issuer documentation that explicitly allows redemption claims to be deferred or cancelled, or satisfied only out of whatever "free assets" the issuer happens to have left, if doing so would not otherwise worsen its own insolvency. In that structure, the token's bankruptcy outcome is closer to an ordinary unsecured bond than to a segregated trust account — and nothing about the token itself tells you which category you are in.

## What actually decides the outcome

Four questions, answerable only from the issuer's own documents, do the real work:

**Is your claim segregated from the issuer's own balance sheet, or is it a claim against the issuer generally?** Segregated, bankruptcy-remote structures are designed to keep customer assets out of the issuer's estate entirely. A general claim stands in line with every other creditor.

**Who holds the underlying asset, and are they independent of the issuer?** A third-party, regulated custodian holding gold, Treasuries, or cash is a different risk than an issuer that verifies its own holdings.

**Can redemption be paused, deferred, or subordinated, and under what conditions?** Some issuer documents build in exactly this right, specifically to protect the issuer's own solvency at the holder's expense.

**What size or notice period does redemption actually require?** A right to redeem that only applies above an institutional minimum, or after a notice period measured in weeks, is a much weaker protection in a fast-moving failure than same-day liquidity.

None of these four answers is visible in a token's ticker, its chain, or the word "tokenized" itself. They are contract terms, and they vary enormously between assets that get described identically in marketing copy.

## What self-custody does and doesn't change

Self-custody is a genuine, specific protection, and it is worth being precise about which risk it actually removes. **You control your Swop wallet: nothing moves without your approval, you can export your private key, and Swop never holds your keys. Wallets run on Privy today.** That removes the risk that an intermediary standing between you and your position blocks it, freezes it, or disappears with it.

What it does not remove is the issuer. As the companion piece on custody above puts it: holding a tokenized asset in your own wallet means you, not a third party, control the token itself — it does not change what the token is a claim on, or how strong that claim is if the issuer behind it fails. Those are two separate risks, solved by two separate things, and conflating them is the most common mistake in how tokenized assets get described.

## Where Swop fits

Swop is not an issuer of tokenized real-world assets, and makes no claim about the bankruptcy structure of any RWA issuer — that is a question for each issuer's own disclosures, not for a wallet that lets you hold and swap the resulting token. What Swop is responsible for is the part under its own control: **tokenized real-world assets that live on Swop's supported chains — such as PAX Gold (PAXG) on Ethereum — can be swapped in the Swop app through its existing routing, the same as any other token on that chain.** Swop runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base, and Polygon, is fully self-custodial, and sponsors gas, so holding one of these tokens does not require first acquiring the chain's native asset to pay a fee.

That combination removes the custodian between you and the token. It is not, and cannot be, a statement about what happens if PAX Gold's issuer, or any other RWA issuer, were to fail — that answer lives entirely in the issuer's own trust structure and documentation, which is exactly why checking it is the point of this post. For completeness: Swop has not commissioned a third-party security audit to date.

## FAQ

### What happens to a tokenized asset if the issuer goes bankrupt?

It depends entirely on the legal structure the issuer chose, not on the blockchain the token runs on. If customer assets sit in a segregated, bankruptcy-remote structure outside the issuer's own estate, a regulator or trustee can typically return them to holders directly. If the token is instead an unsecured claim against the issuer, holders compete with the issuer's other creditors in an ordinary bankruptcy, and that claim can be paused, reduced, or subordinated under the token's own terms.

### Does holding a tokenized asset in my own wallet protect me if the issuer fails?

No. Self-custody protects you from a custodian or exchange blocking, freezing, or losing your access to the token. It does not protect you from the issuer failing, because the token is a claim on that issuer's promise, and the promise does not get stronger because you hold the key to the wallet it sits in.

### How is PAX Gold protected if Paxos becomes insolvent?

Paxos says customer assets are held segregated and bankruptcy-remote, never commingled with its own corporate funds. Under its former New York limited-purpose trust charter it said an insolvency would bypass ordinary bankruptcy, with the NYDFS Superintendent returning custodied assets to owners from Paxos’s books and records. Paxos says it completed a conversion to a national trust bank charter on December 12, 2025 and now operates as Paxos Trust Company, N.A., with PAXG issued by that entity. The OCC’s action that day was a conditional approval, and its decision lists a Conversion Completion Acknowledgement as the step that authorises the converted bank to begin business; we found no OCC notice confirming that step, and a February 2026 OCC decision still refers to the Paxos conversion as a conditional approval. So which charter governs a PAXG holder’s claim today cannot be settled from either party’s public materials. That is this post’s argument in miniature, not a footnote to it.

### What should I check before trusting a tokenized asset's issuer?

Whether your claim is segregated and bankruptcy-remote or a general unsecured claim; whether the custodian holding the underlying asset is independent of the issuer; whether redemption can be paused, deferred, or subordinated, and under what conditions; and what minimum size or notice period redemption actually requires. Those answers are in the issuer's documentation, not in the word "tokenized."

# Somebody made gold in a reactor

A fusion startup says it turned mercury into gold. The quantities are trivial and the tonnage is simulated — but it exposes something about what gold’s scarcity ever rested on, and why scarcity enforced by a rule is a different kind of thing entirely.

ST [Swop Team](https://www.swopme.co/blog/authors/swop-team) Oct 27, 2026 Updated Oct 27, 2026 8 min read Copy link [X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Gold%20was%20never%20scarce%20by%20promise.%20Only%20by%20difficulty.&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fgold-fusion-blockspace-scarcity) [Farcaster](https://warpcast.com/~/compose?text=Gold%20was%20never%20scarce%20by%20promise&embeds[]=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fgold-fusion-blockspace-scarcity)

Contents What was actually announced The numbers, at the right scale What gold’s scarcity was made of Scarcity by rule The honest counterweight Why this is the interesting rush FAQ

Alchemists spent two thousand years trying to make gold and failed, and we took the wrong lesson from it.

The lesson we took was that gold is scarce. The lesson available was narrower: nobody had worked out how yet.

## What was actually announced

On **21 October 2026**, Marathon Fusion said it had produced stable gold from mercury using fusion neutrons — at roughly**ten times** the quantity CERN recorded in 2025. The demonstration reportedly took place in September.

The physics is not exotic. Fast neutrons from deuterium–tritium fusion strike mercury-198; it becomes mercury-197; that decays to gold-197, which is ordinary, stable, indistinguishable gold. The mercury sits in the reactor blanket, the same place the reaction breeds its own tritium fuel.

Now the caveats, because they are load-bearing and most coverage skipped them. The company published **gamma-ray spectra but no mass, no purity figure and no cost.** The spectra do not establish how much gold was made, how pure it was, or whether any of it scales. At the time of reporting it had not been independently verified. This is an announcement, not a result you can check.

## The numbers, at the right scale

It is worth putting all of this on one axis, because the headline and the reality are several orders of magnitude apart.

CERN’s ALICE experiment produced roughly **29 picograms** of gold across four years of running the Large Hadron Collider. Ten times a picogram-scale result is still a picogram-scale result.

The tonnage figures everyone quoted come from somewhere else entirely: a 2025 paper modelling about **2 tonnes of gold per gigawatt of thermal power per year**. The flashier “5,000 kg a year” number is derived from a 1.5 GW thermal simulation producing 2,953 kg a year, restated per gigawatt of electrical output — a different denominator, which is how a modelled 2 becomes a marketed 5.

Those are simulations of a plant nobody has built. Marathon’s current reactor runs at around **one kilowatt** of fusion power. That is a millionth of a gigawatt.

Against that: global gold mine supply was about **3,672 tonnes in 2025** on World Gold Council figures — a record. The US Geological Survey puts the same year nearer 3,300 tonnes, and the gap is a methodology difference worth knowing about rather than averaging away. Either way, a hypothetical gigawatt-scale plant producing 2 tonnes a year would add well under a tenth of one percent of annual supply.

**The gold price is not under threat from this.** Anyone telling you otherwise is running ahead of the data. What changed is not the supply. It is the category.

Sources: CERN ALICE; Marathon Fusion’s 21 Oct 2026 announcement and its 2025 modelling paper; World Gold Council and USGS.

## What gold’s scarcity was made of

Here is the part worth sitting with, and it has nothing to do with whether this particular startup is right.

Roughly **212,000 tonnes** of gold have ever been mined. Nobody promised that. There is no protocol, no issuer, no document anywhere committing the universe to that number or any other. Gold’s scarcity is an observation about how hard it has been to get more — and every observation of that kind is a statement about current cost, not about permanence.

That has always been true. What makes this month interesting is that it stopped being purely theoretical. The constraint on making gold was never a law forbidding it; it was an energy bill nobody could pay. Energy bills move.

So the honest description of gold is not “scarce forever.” It is: **scarce as long as making it costs more than buying it.** That is a real property, it has held for all of recorded history, and it is probably good for a while yet. It is just a different kind of claim than most people think they are making when they say gold is scarce.

## Scarcity by rule

Which brings us to the thing this blog actually cares about.

Blockspace — room in a block to put a transaction — is also scarce, and it is scarce for an entirely different reason. Not because producing more is expensive, but because **a rule says how much there is**. The amount per block is a parameter. It is published in advance, enforced by every node running the software, and checkable by anyone who cares to look.

You do not have to trust an assay, a vault or a mint. You do not have to believe anybody’s cost estimate. The supply is a number in a specification that thousands of independent machines agree on, and if it changed you could see it change.

That is a genuinely different foundation. One scarcity rests on difficulty, which falls. The other rests on agreement, which holds exactly as long as the agreement does.

Neither is permanent. The difference is whether you would be able to see it go.

## The honest counterweight

If the argument stopped there it would be a sales pitch, so here is the other half.

**A rule is only as durable as the people who can change it.** Parameters get changed. Chains fork. Governance votes pass. Plenty of networks have altered supply schedules, block sizes and fee mechanics, and some did it for excellent reasons. “Enforced by consensus” means exactly that — the consensus can decide otherwise.

So rule-based scarcity is not stronger in some absolute sense. It is differently fragile. A cost curve erodes quietly over decades and you learn about it from a press release, which is roughly what just happened with gold. A parameter change has to be proposed, argued over in public and adopted by people who each choose whether to run the new software. Both can fail. One of them fails where you can watch.

And a rule you cannot audit is worth nothing at all, which is why the verifiability matters more than the number. A supply cap you have to take someone’s word for is just an issuer’s promise wearing a technical costume — a point [we have made before about tokenized assets](https://www.swopme.co/blog/tokenized-isnt-the-same-as-yours).

## Why this is the interesting rush

Call it a gold rush if you like, but notice what is actually being claimed.

In an actual gold rush, people raced to a place because the resource was physically there and whoever dug first got it. The scarcity was geological and the claim was a hole in the ground. What is being competed for now is room in a ledger — and the claim is not a shovel, it is a rule that everyone can read.

That is a strange and underrated shift. For the whole history of money, the hardest thing about a scarce asset was proving the scarcity: assays, vaults, audits, trusted mints, and a long tail of people who turned out to be lying about what was in the basement. Scarcity you can verify yourself, without trusting the person telling you about it, is new. It is newer than crypto prices, and it will matter longer.

None of which makes anything a good investment, and we are not telling you to buy anything. The useful takeaway is a question to ask of whatever you hold: **what actually enforces its scarcity — physics, cost, a rule, or somebody’s promise — and what would have to happen for that to stop working?**

For gold, the answer turned out to be “a sufficiently cheap neutron source.” That is much further away than the headlines implied. It is also no longer hypothetical, which it was a month ago.

You control your Swop wallet: nothing moves without your approval, you can export your private key, and Swop never holds your keys. Wallets run on Privy today, and Swop runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base and Polygon. Tokenized real-world assets on those chains, PAX Gold among them, can be swapped in the app through its existing routing like any other token. Whether you want to hold the metal, the blockspace, or neither, the part we think is worth insisting on is that you can check what you hold and move it without asking anyone.

## FAQ

### Has someone actually made gold in a fusion reactor?

Marathon Fusion announced on 21 October 2026 that it produced stable gold from mercury using fusion neutrons, at about ten times what CERN recorded in 2025. Treat it carefully: the company published gamma-ray spectra but no mass, no purity and no cost, and it had not been independently verified at the time of reporting. The mechanism is real physics; the quantity and the scaling are not established.

### Does this threaten the gold price?

Not on today’s evidence. The tonnage figures are simulations of plants nobody has built — about 2 tonnes per gigawatt-thermal per year in the 2025 paper — against roughly 3,672 tonnes of mine supply in 2025 (World Gold Council; USGS says nearer 3,300). The current reactor is around one kilowatt. The principle moved; the supply did not.

### What is the difference between gold's scarcity and blockspace scarcity?

Gold is scarce because making it has been too hard and too expensive — an observation, not a promise. Nobody guaranteed the total would stop near 212,000 tonnes. Blockspace is scarce because a rule says so: a parameter, published in advance, enforced by consensus and checkable by anyone. One depends on difficulty, which falls. The other depends on agreement, which can be renegotiated but not quietly eroded.

### Isn't rule-based scarcity just as fragile?

Differently fragile. Rules get changed by whoever controls them — forks, parameter changes, governance votes — and many chains have changed theirs. The difference is visibility: a cost curve erodes silently and you find out afterwards, while a parameter change has to be proposed and adopted in public. Neither is permanent. One you can watch.

### What should I take from this?

That “scarce” is not one property. Ask what enforces the scarcity of anything you hold — physics, cost, a rule, or an issuer’s promise — and what would have to happen for that enforcement to stop. The answers differ, and so do the ways they fail.

# Remittances: the real test for tokenized money

Stablecoins move value across a border in seconds, and that's the proof crypto points to when it calls remittances a test case it's passing. But a remittance isn't finished until that balance becomes cash someone can spend — and that half of the trip hasn't gotten any faster.

ST [Swop Team](https://www.swopme.co/blog/authors/swop-team) Oct 20, 2026 Updated Oct 20, 2026 6 min read Copy link [X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Remittances%3A%20the%20real%20test%20for%20tokenized%20money&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fremittances-tokenized-money) [Farcaster](https://warpcast.com/~/compose?text=Remittances%3A%20the%20real%20test%20for%20tokenized%20money&embeds[]=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fremittances-tokenized-money)

Contents Two legs, one word What the wire actually proved The leg nobody tokenized Where it's already a clean pass Where Swop sits in this FAQ

Tokenized money — stablecoins moving on public blockchains — settles a cross-border transfer in seconds, for a fee far below what a bank charges, and that is the part crypto points to when it calls remittances a test case it is passing. The test actually has two legs. The wire is solved. The cash-out — turning that balance into spendable local currency — still runs through the same slow, fee-taking network it always has, which is why a transfer that settles on-chain in seconds can still take a recipient days to actually receive.

## Two legs, one word

“Remittance” describes the whole trip: money leaves a sender in one country and becomes usable money for a recipient in another. Historically one rail did both jobs at once — a bank wire or a Western Union counter moved the value and handed over something spendable at the other end, because there was no way to separate the two.

A stablecoin transfer separates them for the first time. It does the first job — moving value across the border — essentially for free and instantly. It does not, by itself, do the second job. A balance of tokenized dollars sitting in a wallet is not the same thing as cash in a recipient's hand or a deposit their bank will accept, and conflating the two is where the “crypto fixed remittances” claim overreaches.

## What the wire actually proved

It is worth being precise about what did get solved, because it is real. The World Bank's [Remittance Prices Worldwide](https://remittanceprices.worldbank.org/node/1) database — which tracks pricing across 377 country corridors, from 48 sending to 111 receiving countries — puts the global average total cost of sending $200 at **6.36% of the amount sent**, in its most recent published survey round (Q3 2025 data). A September 2026 [Solana Foundation report on money movement](https://solana.com/news/report-stablecoins-are-reshaping-remittances), looking specifically at legacy-rail corridors from the US to Mexico, Brazil, Nigeria, the Philippines and India, cites an average fee of**6.49% on a $200 transfer**and settlement times of**three to five business days**. Worth noting what that fee figure is: 6.49% is the World Bank's own global average for a $200 transfer one quarter earlier, so it corroborates nothing independently — it is the same series, read at a different point. (Solana Foundation is a blockchain-industry publisher with an evident interest in this comparison; its settlement-time range is reported here as its own claim, not independently verified.)

World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide; Solana Foundation, “An Evolution of Money Movement” (Sept 2026). The right-hand box describes the wire only.

That gap — a fee measured in whole percentage points and days, against a fee measured in fractions of a cent and seconds — is genuinely the thing crypto changed. It is just not the whole remittance.

## The leg nobody tokenized

Most remittance recipients cannot spend a stablecoin balance directly. They need local cash, or a deposit their own bank or mobile-money account will accept, because that is what pays rent and buys groceries where they live. Getting from a wallet balance to that point requires an off-ramp: a local agent, an exchange, or a payout partner with liquidity in the local currency and the compliance work — identity checks, sanctions screening — already done on the receiving end. None of that moved on-chain. Only the transfer between the two ends of it did, which is why the fee and the delay that used to sit on the whole trip now concentrate almost entirely on that last mile.

The clearest evidence of this is who is adopting the technology, and how. Both incumbents now issue their own stablecoin: Western Union launched **USDPT**on Solana in May 2026, and MoneyGram launched**MGUSD** on Stellar in June 2026. Both are positioned first as settlement assets — moving dollars across their own networks around the clock instead of waiting on correspondent banks — and both now put a dollar-denominated balance in front of customers too. MoneyGram's sits in a self-custodial wallet inside its own app, letting a recipient hold dollars and convert to local currency on demand.

That second part cuts against the lazy version of this argument, so it is worth stating plainly: the incumbents are not only using stablecoins out of sight. But look at what neither of them retired. MoneyGram's balance still converts on demand through its network of roughly 500,000 retail locations, because cash is what a recipient who needs cash actually needs. The wire between their own accounts got replaced. The payout network got kept — and the payout network, not the wire, is the expensive thing to run. That is a meaningful signal about where the actual cost still lives.

The honest version A remittance that “settles instantly” on-chain and then sits for three days waiting on a local payout partner has not gotten faster from the sender's point of view. It has moved the slow part to a stage of the trip that is harder to see.

Channel averages, World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide (Q3 2025 data). The spread tracks how much cash the channel touches — not how fast the wire is.

## Where it's already a clean pass

None of this means the test case fails everywhere — it means the test case is conditional. When a recipient is willing and able to hold the stablecoin itself, there is no second leg to solve, because the transfer is the payment. A freelancer invoicing a client abroad in USDC, a small merchant settling with a cross-border supplier, a diaspora saver who already keeps a dollar-denominated balance rather than the local currency — for all of them, the wire is the whole trip, and tokenized money passes outright: instant, near-free, and finished the moment it arrives.

That version of a cross-border transfer — fund it once, let the recipient receive it directly into their own wallet rather than through an intermediary account — is closer to how a [claim-link transfer](https://www.swopme.co/blog/send-crypto-with-a-link) works than how a traditional remittance works, and it is the shape the rest of this gets judged against as off-ramp networks slowly improve.

## Where Swop sits in this

Swop is built for the leg that is already solved, and is honest about not being a cash-out network. You control your Swop wallet: nothing moves without your approval, you can export your private key, and Swop never holds your keys. Wallets run on Privy today. That means a transfer that lands in a Swop wallet is immediately the recipient's, not a balance an intermediary is holding on their behalf. Transactions on Swop are gas-sponsored, so neither side needs to hold SOL or ETH just to move the money, and Swop runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base, and Polygon, so the wire itself isn't tied to a single network's fees or congestion.

That is one leg of the trip, stated plainly as one leg. Whether a given remittance also needs a cash-out still depends on whether the recipient can use a dollar-denominated balance directly — the question this piece spent its length on, not a question any wallet answers by existing.

## FAQ

### Do stablecoins actually make remittances cheaper?

For the transfer itself, yes — moving a stablecoin across a public blockchain costs a small, predictable network fee regardless of distance. But the cost most people measure is the whole trip: sender to recipient, in spendable local currency. The World Bank's most recent published round puts that whole-trip average at 6.36% of a $200 transfer, and it has sat above 6% for years, because the fee is mostly charged on the cash-out leg, not the wire.

### Haven't Western Union and MoneyGram already solved this with their own stablecoins?

Not the cash-out leg. Western Union launched USDPT on Solana in May 2026 and MoneyGram launched MGUSD on Stellar in June 2026, and both go further than back-end settlement — MoneyGram's sits in a self-custodial wallet in its own app, so a recipient can hold dollars instead of converting immediately. But neither company retired its payout network, and MoneyGram's dollar balance still converts to local currency on demand across roughly 500,000 retail locations. The stablecoin replaced the wire between their own accounts; the agent network that turns a balance into spendable cash is still there, still staffed, and still priced.

### If the wire is instant, why do remittances still take days?

Because the wire and the payout are two different jobs. A stablecoin transfer settles in seconds. Turning that balance into cash a recipient can spend at a shop, or a deposit their local bank will accept, requires an off-ramp — a local agent, exchange or payout partner with liquidity, compliance checks and operating hours in the receiving country. None of that moved on-chain; only the transfer between the two ends of it did.

### When does a stablecoin remittance skip the cash-out problem entirely?

When the recipient is willing and able to hold the stablecoin itself, rather than needing it converted to local cash — a freelancer being paid in USDC, a merchant settling with a cross-border supplier, or anyone who already spends or saves in a dollar-denominated balance. In that case there is no second leg: the transfer that lands in the wallet is the payment, and the test case is a clean pass.

# Starbucks runs a $1.7 billion float on gift cards

The gift card is the most underrated product in retail. It is paid for before anything is handed over, and it gives someone a reason to walk back through your door. Geo Bucks, Drops and Launchpad put that same mechanic behind any counter — without the fifteen years of engineering.

ST [Swop Team](https://www.swopme.co/blog/authors/swop-team) Oct 15, 2026 Updated Oct 15, 2026 8 min read Copy link [X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Starbucks%20runs%20a%20%241.7%20billion%20float%20on%20gift%20cards.%20Your%20counter%20can%20run%20one%20too.&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fgeo-bucks-drops-store-credit) [Farcaster](https://warpcast.com/~/compose?text=Starbucks%20runs%20a%20%241.7B%20float%20on%20gift%20cards&embeds[]=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fgeo-bucks-drops-store-credit)

Contents The most underrated product in retail What the float is really worth Why your corner shop never got one Credit that lives at a place Setting it up The honest limits FAQ

A coffee company is sitting on roughly **$1.7 billion** of other people’s money, and nobody thinks of it as a financial institution.

As of June 28, 2026, Starbucks reported about **$1.74 billion**in stored value card and loyalty deferred revenue. In that quarter alone customers loaded roughly**$3.67 billion** onto cards and Stars. People hand over money, and sometime later they get coffee.

That is a gift card programme. It is the most underrated product in retail, and for most of the last twenty years it has been effectively unavailable to anyone who isn’t a chain.

## The most underrated product in retail

Think about what a gift card actually does for the business that issues it.

It is **paid for before anything is delivered.** A normal sale converts inventory into cash at the moment of the transaction. A prepaid balance collects the cash first and delivers the product later, sometimes much later, sometimes in a different quarter.

It is **spent where it was issued.** A customer holding $25 of credit at your counter is not comparing you to the place across the street on price. The decision was already made, and it was made in your favour.

And it **creates a reason to return.** This is the part that matters most and gets discussed least. A balance is an open loop. People close open loops.

## What the float is really worth

Here is where the popular version of this story goes wrong, so let us be exact.

The money is **a liability, not profit.** On the balance sheet it sits as deferred revenue because it is customer money owed in product. Starbucks has not earned $1.7 billion; it owes $1.7 billion in coffee. Recognising that correctly is the difference between a funding advantage and an accounting fiction.

What a large, steady balance does give you is **working capital that costs nothing to borrow.** Money received months before the product is handed over funds the business in the interval, and it carries no interest and no covenant.

The other half of the folklore is breakage — the balances nobody ever redeems. It is real, and it is far smaller than people assume: Starbucks recognised **$212.7 million** of breakage in fiscal 2022, against card loads in the billions. Meaningful, but a rounding error next to redeemed volume.

Which is worth saying plainly, because it changes what you should build: **a credit programme designed around money people forget is both bad business and bad faith.** The durable value is the visits. Someone with a balance at your counter comes back to your counter.

The money is a liability the whole way round. The asset is step three happening again and again.

## Why your corner shop never got one

None of the above is a secret. The reason the bakery on your street doesn’t run a stored value programme is that the machinery has always been out of reach.

To do it properly you need a ledger of balances, a way to issue credit, a way to accept it at the till, somewhere for the liability to live, and the ability to settle between locations. For a chain that is a project. For a single counter it has never been worth it, so the category belonged to companies with an engineering department.

What changes that is not a clever marketing idea. It is that the ledger already exists, and a merchant can issue against it without building anything.

## Credit that lives at a place

Three pieces on Swop do this, and they fit together in one line.

**Launchpad** is where you launch a token. That is the instrument — the thing that represents credit, or a community token with a fixed supply that trades.

**Geo Bucks** are store credit denominated in the obvious way: one Buck is a dollar of credit at your own counter. They are redeemable only at stores you register, so the credit is yours and cannot be spent against someone else’s till. When someone receives Bucks, the credit lands in their Swop wallet. Customers can also simply buy store credit — which is the gift card, rebuilt.

**Drops** are the part with no high-street equivalent. A Drop is credit placed at a location. You create one for your counter, people nearby see it on the map, and they claim it in person by scanning the counter code. Each Drop pays out of a Geo Bucks budget you fund in advance — and creating a Drop moves no tokens by itself; it just sets the budget that claims draw from.

That last mechanic is worth sitting with. A coupon is something a customer carries to you, and most of them never do. A Drop is something that **exists at a place and has to be collected there**. The redemption and the visit are the same event. You are not buying awareness and hoping it converts into footfall; the footfall is the conversion.

And unlike a discount, a Drop doesn’t train people to wait for a sale. It puts credit in their wallet that is only worth anything at your door.

Launch the token, fund the budget, place the Drop. Creating a Drop moves no tokens on its own.

## Setting it up

In the order the dashboard expects:

**Launch a token** from Launchpad. Nothing downstream works until there is an instrument to denominate credit in.

**Register your stores.** Bucks are redeemable only at locations you register, so this is what makes the credit specifically yours. It is also what stops it leaking anywhere else.

**Fund a Geo Bucks budget** — the pot that claims are paid from. You decide the size, and that number is your exposure.

**Create a Drop** against the budget, pointed at your counter. People nearby see it on the map; they turn up and scan to claim.

It runs from the Swop dashboard at [swopme.app](https://www.swopme.app), and the customer side needs nothing but the Swop app. No terminal, no integration, no separate gift card vendor.

## The honest limits

Three, and they are the sort a vendor usually leaves out.

**Prepaid credit is a liability, and it is regulated.** When you issue store credit you owe it. Many jurisdictions have rules about gift cards and stored value — expiry limits, disclosure, and unclaimed-property rules among them — and they differ considerably by country and by state. This post describes a mechanic. It is not legal or accounting advice, and you should find out what applies where you trade before you issue at scale.

**Your float is only as useful as your inventory.** The Starbucks version works because people want coffee repeatedly and predictably. Credit at a counter nobody visits twice is just a slower refund.

**And Swop has not commissioned a third-party security audit to date.** That is true of the platform underneath all of this, and it belongs in the decision.

What’s left after those caveats is still the interesting bit. The prepaid balance is one of the few mechanics in retail that improves working capital and footfall at the same time, and until recently it was reserved for companies that could afford to build it. Now it takes an afternoon.

## FAQ

### What are Geo Bucks?

Store credit you issue yourself. One Buck is a dollar of credit at your own counter, redeemable only at stores you register. When someone receives them the credit lands in their Swop wallet, and customers can also buy store credit directly.

### What is a Drop, and how is it different from a coupon?

A Drop is credit placed at a location. You create one for your counter, people nearby see it on the map, and they claim it in person by scanning the counter code. A coupon is something a customer carries to you; a Drop exists at a place and has to be collected there — so the redemption and the visit are the same event.

### Why do gift cards help beyond the sale?

Prepaid balances are cash received before goods are delivered. Starbucks reported about $1.74 billion of stored value and loyalty deferred revenue as of June 28, 2026, and loaded roughly $3.67 billion in that quarter. But it is a liability, not profit — customer money owed in product. The durable advantage is behavioural: a balance is a reason to come back, to your counter specifically.

### Isn’t the real benefit the cards nobody redeems?

That is breakage, and it is smaller than the folklore. Starbucks recognised $212.7 million in fiscal 2022 against billions in loads. Designing a credit programme around balances you hope go unused is bad business and bad faith. Run it for the visits.

### What do I need to set it up?

Launch a token from Launchpad, register the stores where credit can be redeemed, fund a Geo Bucks budget, then create a Drop against it. Creating a Drop moves no tokens by itself — it sets the budget claims are paid from. It all runs from the Swop dashboard.

### Are there rules about issuing store credit?

Yes, and they vary by jurisdiction — expiry limits, disclosure, unclaimed-property rules. This post describes a mechanic, not a legal opinion. Check what applies where you trade.

# El Dorado is live in beta

A virtual world built on Swop, open now in beta. Sign in with your swop.id, put on a headset if you have one, and walk around a world you entered with keys you actually hold. New improvements every week.

ST [Swop Team](https://www.swopme.co/blog/authors/swop-team) Oct 14, 2026 Updated Oct 14, 2026 7 min read Copy link [X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=El%20Dorado%20is%20live%20in%20beta%20%E2%80%94%20a%20virtual%20world%20you%20enter%20with%20a%20wallet%20you%20hold%20the%20keys%20to.&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fel-dorado-virtual-world-beta) [Farcaster](https://warpcast.com/~/compose?text=El%20Dorado%20is%20live%20in%20beta&embeds[]=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Fel-dorado-virtual-world-beta)

Contents Getting in Why we built it this way The clearest example is a city What changes in El Dorado What we're not claiming It's a beta, and it moves weekly Come in FAQ

**El Dorado is open.** It is a virtual world built on Swop, it is live in beta right now at [swopme.co/eldorado](https://www.swopme.co/eldorado), and you can be inside it in about a minute.

You can walk in on your laptop, or put on a headset and walk in properly. What you need is a swop.id — the identity you already have if you use the Swop app. There is no new account to make and no password to invent.

## Getting in

Three steps, and the third one is optional.

**1. Open [swopme.co/eldorado](https://www.swopme.co/eldorado).** It asks you to sign in with your swop.id from the Swop app. If you don’t have one yet, claim it in the app first — it takes a moment and it is the same id you use everywhere else in Swop.

**2. Approve it on your phone.** Open the Swop app, go to Wallet settings → Wallet connections, scan the code on screen, approve. You’re in.

**3. If you have a headset, pair it.** You never type a password with a controller. Sign in on your phone, then enter the short code the headset shows you — or scan from the headset directly. Then you are standing in it rather than looking at it.

## Why we built it this way

Here is the part that makes El Dorado different from every virtual world you have been in before, and it is worth two minutes.

In almost every game you have played, **you do not own your stuff.** You hold a licence to use it. The terms usually say so in plain words. The publisher can close your account, and when that happens your inventory goes with it — not because anyone stole it, but because it was never in your hands to begin with. It lived in their database, and your account was the key to it.

Most publishers also forbid selling or moving items outside their own systems. So the way out is controlled by the same people who control the way in.

The difference is custody, not graphics. Note the last line on the right — it is the honest limit of the claim.

## The clearest example is a city

A few years ago, some developers rebuilt Grand Theft Auto III and Vice City from the outside — reverse-engineering them so the games would run properly on modern machines. The projects shipped no game content at all. **You had to own the original game for them to work.**

They were taken down anyway. Take-Two filed a DMCA notice in February 2021 and GitHub pulled the code. A counter-notice brought a fork back. A lawsuit followed that September, the projects came down again in October, and the month after that Take-Two released its own remasters of both games. It was later settled.

Open the original repository today and you get **“451 — Unavailable for Legal Reasons”**, an error code originally meant for censorship. We checked the morning this went up.

You can take either side of that fight. The bit that matters here is simpler: **every person who bought that game still only had a licence to it.** The city they drove around in existed because someone else allowed it to. That is the normal condition of virtual worlds, and most people have never had a reason to notice.

## What changes in El Dorado

You arrive holding your own keys.

You control your Swop wallet: nothing moves without your approval, you can export your private key, and Swop never holds your keys. Wallets run on Privy today. Your way in is something you control, not an account someone else can switch off.

A few practical consequences:

**No buying a token before you can do anything.** Transactions on Swop are gas-sponsored. You don’t need to hold SOL or ETH to transact — Swop covers the network fee and absorbs it rather than passing it on.

**It isn’t trapped in one world.** The wallet you walk in with is the same one you use across Swop, which runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base and Polygon — not a balance that only means something inside one company’s game.

**Losing your phone isn’t losing anything.** Log in with your email on a new phone and your wallet comes back. You can also export your private key and open your assets in a completely different wallet.

## What we’re not claiming

Two honest limits, because the overclaim here is easy and we’d rather you hear it from us.

**Self-custody isn’t the same as legal ownership.** Holding something in a wallet you control changes what can be done to your access — it can’t be quietly frozen, and it isn’t stuck inside one platform’s trading system. It does not settle what legal rights you have in a virtual item. That still depends on the terms you agreed to and the country you’re in, and the law there is genuinely unsettled. Anyone telling you a wallet turns a game item into property in the legal sense is skipping a step.

**And holding your own keys means holding your own keys.** Email recovery and key export exist for a reason, but the honest version of “nobody can take this from you” is “nobody can get it back for you either.”

One more, while we’re here: Swop has not commissioned a third-party security audit to date. That is true of the platform El Dorado runs on, and you should weigh it when deciding how much to bring into a beta.

## It’s a beta, and it moves every week

We mean beta literally, not as a legal cushion. Things will change under you. Some things will break. Features will move or disappear.

**Improvements ship every week**, so the El Dorado you walk into this Monday is not the one that will be there next Monday. That is the point of opening it now rather than later — we would rather build it in front of you.

A beta label describes the state of the software. It does not move the consequences onto the person using it.

Beta describes the state of the software. It doesn’t move the consequences of rough edges onto you. If something behaves badly in there, that’s ours to fix.

## Come in

[swopme.co/eldorado](https://www.swopme.co/eldorado). Bring a swop.id, or claim one in the Swop app on the way. If you want the longer argument for why entering a world with keys you hold is different in kind from entering one with an account, [we wrote that up here](https://www.swopme.co/blog/tokenized-isnt-the-same-as-yours).

## FAQ

### What is El Dorado?

A virtual world built on Swop, live in beta at [swopme.co/eldorado](https://www.swopme.co/eldorado). You enter it by signing in with your swop.id from the Swop app rather than by making a new game account.

### How do I get in?

Open swopme.co/eldorado, sign in with your swop.id, and approve it in the Swop app (Wallet settings → Wallet connections → scan the code). On a headset, sign in on your phone and enter the code the headset shows you — no typing with a controller.

### Do I need crypto experience or a seed phrase?

No. You need a swop.id, claimed in the Swop app. You control your Swop wallet and Swop never holds your keys, but you sign in with your identity rather than by managing a seed phrase. Transactions are gas-sponsored too, so you don’t need to hold SOL or ETH to transact.

### Does this mean I legally own my virtual items?

Not automatically. In most games virtual items are granted under a limited licence rather than sold as property, and publishers can close accounts. Holding something in a wallet you control changes what can be done to your access — it can’t be quietly frozen and isn’t confined to one platform’s trading system — but legal rights in virtual goods still depend on the terms and your jurisdiction. Those are two different questions, and we’re only claiming the first.

### What does “beta” mean here?

That it changes under you. Improvements ship every week, so expect rough edges and expect things to move. Beta describes the state of the software; it doesn’t make the rough edges your problem.

Beta

# Tokenized isn’t the same as yours

Tokenized real-world assets passed $32 billion this year. The largest category of them reverts if you send it to a wallet nobody approved — and that is a design choice, not a technical limit. Custody is the variable that decides what tokenization is actually for.

ST [Swop Team](https://www.swopme.co/blog/authors/swop-team) Oct 13, 2026 Updated Oct 13, 2026 9 min read Copy link [X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Tokenized%20isn%27t%20the%20same%20as%20yours.&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Ftokenized-isnt-the-same-as-yours) [Farcaster](https://warpcast.com/~/compose?text=Tokenized%20isn%27t%20the%20same%20as%20yours&embeds[]=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.swopme.co%2Fblog%2Ftokenized-isnt-the-same-as-yours)

Contents $32 billion, and most of it can’t move The allowlist is the product Gold took a different road Custody is a dial Why the dial decides who gets in What self-custody doesn’t fix Where Swop fits FAQ

There is a sentence that gets repeated at every tokenization conference, and it is almost right: put the asset on a chain and anyone can own a piece of it.

Almost. The chain is the easy part. What determines whether anyone can own a piece of it is a decision the issuer makes about custody — and in 2026, for the biggest slice of the market, that decision has gone the other way.

## $32 billion, and most of it can’t move

The numbers are real and they are growing fast. On-chain value across tokenized real-world assets reached about **$32 billion at the end of June 2026**, excluding stablecoins — up from roughly $11.8 billion a year earlier, according to [RWA.xyz](https://app.rwa.xyz/). US Treasuries are the largest single category by a wide margin. Commodities are a much smaller slice, and gold is the large majority of that slice. Tokenized equities are small but growing quickly; tokenized real estate, despite being the example everybody reaches for, is still a rounding error.

One caution about those headline figures, because they get quoted loosely: trackers publish both the value of tokens actually distributed on-chain and the much larger value of assets merely represented there, and the gap between those two measures is enormous. Totals that fold in stablecoins are larger again and not comparable at all. Growth this fast attracts round numbers, and the round numbers are usually measuring different things.

But the size of the market is not the interesting fact. This is: **if you buy the largest category of tokenized asset and then try to move it to a wallet you control, the transfer fails.**

## The allowlist is the product

Tokenized Treasury funds — BlackRock’s BUIDL, [Ondo’s OUSG](https://ondo.finance/ousg), and their peers — run an on-chain allowlist. The issuer, or its transfer agent ( [Securitize](https://securitize.io/), in BUIDL’s case), adds a wallet address to that list only after the holder behind it clears identity checks, sanctions screening and investor-eligibility verification. A transfer to an address that is not on the list does not get flagged for review later. It reverts at the contract level, immediately, as a matter of code.

The practical consequence is worth stating plainly: move BUIDL to a new self-custody wallet and the transfer fails unless that new address has been approved first. Peer-to-peer transfer to someone who is not on the list is not difficult or discouraged. It is impossible by construction.

It is important to be fair about why. These are regulated securities offerings, and the exemptions they rely on genuinely restrict who may hold them — BUIDL is offered to qualified purchasers, a bar that in practice means institutional-scale money. The allowlist is simply how that legal restriction gets enforced in code instead of in a filing cabinet. It is doing a real job, honestly.

The point is not that the gate is illegitimate. The point is that **the gate now travels with the asset**. In the old world, the restriction lived in your relationship with a broker. Tokenizing it did not remove it; it compiled it into the thing itself.

## Gold took a different road

Compare Paxos’s [PAX Gold](https://www.paxos.com/pax-gold). It is an ordinary ERC-20 token: any Ethereum wallet can receive it, hold it and send it on, with no approval step and no list to be added to. A person with a phone and no banking relationship at all can hold a token backed by allocated gold.

That is a meaningfully different design, and it is worth not overselling it. PAXG is permissionlessly held, but it is not an unowned bearer instrument. The contract is centrally administered: per [Paxos’s own documentation](https://docs.paxos.com/), there are roles that can mint and burn supply, pause transfers and freeze balances where law requires it. And redemption — the thing that makes the token worth anything — runs through Paxos’s verified customers, with minimum sizes that put physical delivery well out of reach of a small holder.

So neither of these assets is simply “yours.” But the difference between them is not cosmetic. In one case you cannot hold the token without permission. In the other you can hold and move it freely, and the issuer’s controls sit at the edges — at issuance, at redemption, and at the legal exceptions. Those are different worlds for anybody who is not already inside the financial system.

Custody is a dial, not a property of being “on-chain.” Every tokenized asset sits somewhere on it, by design.

## Custody is a dial

This is the part that gets lost. “On-chain” is not one thing. Every tokenized asset makes two separate choices, and only one of them is about blockchains:

**Can the holder be anyone?** Either the token enforces a list of approved addresses, or it does not. This is a binary, it is written in the contract, and it decides whether participation requires a relationship with the issuer.

**Can the issuer intervene after the fact?** Pause, freeze, mint, burn, upgrade. Almost every asset-backed token keeps some of these powers, and for assets with a legal claim behind them, it is hard to see how it could be otherwise.

A tokenized Treasury fund answers “no” to the first and “yes” to the second. It is, functionally, a faster ledger at the same custodian — which is a genuine improvement for the institutions using it, and almost no change at all for everyone else. Tokenized gold answers “yes” and “yes.” A native crypto asset answers “yes” and “no,” and pays for it by having no redemption claim at all.

None of these is the right answer in the abstract. But notice that the technology does not pick. The issuer does.

## Why the dial decides who gets in

Here is why this matters more than the market-size chart.

The standard argument for tokenization is inclusion: fractional ownership, lower minimums, global access, a market open on a Sunday. Every part of that argument depends on the first dial being set to “anyone can hold it.” If the token requires an approved address, then the people it reaches are the people who can already get approved — which is roughly the set of people who could already buy the asset.

A tokenized Treasury fund with a qualified-purchaser gate and an institutional minimum has not widened access to Treasuries. It has made Treasury settlement faster for people who already hold Treasuries. That is worth doing. It is just not the thing the inclusion argument promised.

Whereas a person with a phone, no bank account and no accredited-investor letter can hold tokenized gold today. Not because gold is special, but because somebody designed that token so the holder did not need permission. That is the whole difference.

The word “tokenized” answers none of these. The issuer’s documentation and the token contract answer all three.

## What self-custody doesn’t fix

It would be easy to end here with self-custody as the answer to everything, and that would be dishonest.

Self-custody removes one specific risk: that an intermediary standing between you and your position blocks it, loses it, or goes away. That is not a small risk, and the last several years have been an extended demonstration of it.

What self-custody does not remove is the issuer. A tokenized gold or Treasury token is a claim. Its value rests on an entity continuing to hold the real asset and continuing to honour redemption. Hold the token in your own wallet and you have removed the custodian; you have not removed the counterparty. And as noted above, redemption usually runs through verified accounts and minimum sizes that a small holder will not clear — so for most people, the practical exit is selling the token to someone else, not redeeming it for the thing.

Self-custody also hands you the key problem. Lose the key and there is no support line that can restore it. That trade-off is the price of the gate being gone, and anyone advocating self-custody who does not say so plainly is selling something.

## Where Swop fits

You control your Swop wallet: nothing moves without your approval, you can export your private key, and Swop never holds your keys. Wallets run on Privy today. That is the side of the dial we build on, and it is a deliberate choice rather than a technical accident.

Concretely: tokenized real-world assets that live on Swop’s supported chains — such as PAX Gold on Ethereum — can be swapped in the Swop app through its existing routing, the same as any other token. Swop runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base and Polygon, and transactions are gas-sponsored, so holding a tokenized asset does not require first acquiring the chain’s native token to pay a fee. Swop covers the network fee; it is a cost Swop absorbs, not a charge passed through to you.

What that adds up to is narrow and worth stating precisely: for the tokenized assets that were designed to be held without permission, Swop lets you hold and move them without a custodian, an approval queue, or a gas balance. It does not get you into an allowlisted fund — nothing can, except being the kind of holder that fund was offered to. And for completeness, in the spirit of the three questions above: Swop has not commissioned a third-party security audit to date.

The broader point is the one worth carrying out of this piece. The tokenization story is usually told as though the chain is the interesting part. It isn’t. The chain is settled technology. The open question for the next decade of this market is which way issuers set the custody dial — and that question is being answered, asset by asset, right now, mostly in favour of the people who were never locked out in the first place.

## FAQ

### If an asset is tokenized, can I hold it in my own wallet?

Sometimes, and it depends entirely on how the issuer designed the token rather than on the chain it runs on. Tokenized Treasury funds such as BUIDL and OUSG operate an on-chain allowlist: a wallet is added only after that holder clears identity, sanctions and investor-eligibility checks, and a transfer to an address that is not on the list fails at the contract level. Moving BUIDL to a new self-custody wallet means getting that new address approved first. Other tokens, such as PAX Gold, can be received and transferred by any ordinary Ethereum wallet with no approval step.

### How big is the tokenized real-world asset market in 2026?

Roughly $32 billion of on-chain value as of the end of June 2026, excluding stablecoins, up from about $11.8 billion a year earlier, per RWA.xyz. US Treasuries are the largest category; commodities are much smaller, and gold is most of that. Compare headline numbers carefully: trackers report both value actually distributed on-chain and the far larger value of assets merely represented there, and totals including stablecoins are not comparable.

### Why do tokenized Treasury funds use an allowlist at all?

Because they are regulated securities offerings and the exemption they rely on limits who may hold them — BUIDL is offered to qualified purchasers, which in practice means institutional-scale investors. The allowlist enforces that restriction in code rather than on paper. It is doing a real job; the point is that the restriction now travels with the token.

### Does self-custody make a tokenized asset risk-free?

No. It removes the risk that an intermediary blocks or loses your access. It does not remove the issuer. A tokenized asset is a claim, and that claim depends on the issuer holding the asset and honouring redemption — and redemption typically requires a verified account and a minimum size a small holder may not meet. Holding it yourself and being able to redeem it yourself are different things.

### What should I check before treating a tokenized asset as mine?

Whether it can be transferred to an address the issuer has not pre-approved; whether the issuer can freeze or pause balances, and under what conditions; and what redemption actually requires. Those answers are in the issuer’s documentation and the token contract, and they vary widely between assets all described as “tokenized.”

Self-custody

### Hold it yourself

Swop is self-custodial, runs on Solana, Ethereum, Base and Polygon, and sponsors gas — so holding a token doesn’t mean first buying one to pay a fee.
